title: John the Evangelist (27 December)
hook: the beloved disciple, the eagle, and the one the fourth Gospel places at the cross

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eve, kept on Christmas Eve in some old calendars. Your line was the first parents. Did you pray, or simply hope, for the whole human family? Day one thousand fifty-seven.

"Lord, who is it?" A question asked at supper on the night before the cross. Jesus has just said that one of the twelve will betray him. Peter wants a name, so he signals to the disciple closest to Jesus, the one leaning against his chest. That disciple leans back and asks the question. The Gospel never gives him a name in that scene. It gives him a description instead. Today, two days after Christmas, the Church keeps the feast of the man tradition says that description belongs to.
screen: `LORD, WHO IS IT?` → `PETER SIGNALS.` → `A HEAD RESTING AGAINST JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the description, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved." The Gospel of John comes back to that description more than once, the disciple whom Jesus loved, and never calls him by name. The Church's tradition identifies him with John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, and names the fourth Gospel after him. Some modern readers wonder whether the beloved disciple was someone else. The text itself leaves him unnamed, and that silence may be the point: a disciple described only by being loved. Then the cross. The fourth Gospel places him there, standing beside the mother of Jesus. Jesus looks at the two of them and says to her, "Woman, behold thy son." And to him, "Behold thy mother." From that hour, the Gospel says, the disciple took her into his own home. Catholic tradition reads that moment as Mary being given to every disciple, not only to one. On Easter morning he runs to the empty tomb with Peter and gets there first. And at the very end, the Gospel says this disciple is the one who bears witness to these things and wrote them down. In Christian art he is often painted with an eagle. Tradition gives each Gospel writer a living creature from the visions of Ezekiel and the Apocalypse, and John gets the eagle; the traditional explanation is that his Gospel flies high from its opening line, In the beginning was the Word. So one man carries both pictures: the eagle soaring, and the head resting quietly on a friend's chest. This week we walked with Nicholas giving in secret, Juan Diego the littlest son, the holy house of Loreto, Lucy's light, Kanty's coat, and our first parents. Today the week ends at the supper table.
screen: `LEANING ON JESUS' BOSOM.` · `A DISCIPLE NAMED ONLY BY LOVE.` · `BEHOLD THY MOTHER.` · `THE EAGLE AND THE RESTING HEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest your head, figuratively, on Christ. Settle somewhere you can lean back, a chair with a high back, a wall, a pillow. Let your head be held by something for a change instead of holding itself up. Notice the weight leave your neck. Then remember the beloved disciple at that table, close enough to whisper. If you pray, you can rest there with Jesus for two minutes without asking for anything at all. If you don't, simply let yourself be held by the chair and the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Evangelist. The disciple whom Jesus loved, as tradition identifies him: at the supper, at the cross, at the tomb, and marked in art by the eagle. Today's word.
Your line: the beloved disciple. Today, when someone says your name, let it remind you that the Gospel named this disciple only by being loved. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint John, apostle and evangelist, on 27 December, inside the Christmas octave; in some places wine is blessed on his day, a custom tied to a story people tell about him.

original.note: Greek of John 13:23: whom Jesus loved. the phrase the Gospel uses instead of a name.

trapdoor: what you thought: John, the apostle who wrote a Gospel.
what it means: the disciple whom Jesus loved, at the supper, the cross and the tomb, whom the Church's tradition identifies as John.
what a scholar hears: the fourth Gospel never names him; the identification with John son of Zebedee is tradition, and some modern readers question it.
